recent_posts.author: Carl
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi @xingtianchunyan and thanks to the committee for the detailed notice.
I want to correct two things in the review, because I think they changed the
outcome, and then report what has changed since the close.
The first is the baseline. The notice cites $1,000 and requires the swap
component. That was the original proposal. On 13 August the committee revised
the scope: RGB++ integration was removed and the grant set to $500 over four
weeks (Spark Program | Fiber RGB++ Swap - #18 by zz_tovarishch). I
accepted in Spark Program | Fiber RGB++ Swap - #19 by Carl,
the plan I was paid against is
Spark Program | Fiber RGB++ Swap - #20 by Carl, and 609,757
CKB was approved on that basis
(Spark Program | Fiber RGB++ Swap - #21 by zz_tovarishch) with 121,952
CKB paid (Spark Program | Fiber RGB++ Swap - #24 by xingtianchunyan).
That four-week plan has no swap in it: design and schema, gossip integration,
discovery with RPC and CLI, then testing, demo and docs. Measured against the
scope the committee set and paid for, all four weeks were delivered.
The second is the artifact. The notice says the delivery was simulated with
hardcoded data and never verified on testnet. That describes the August
scaffold from Spark Program | Fiber RGB++ Swap - #10 by Carl,
whose leap logic I said at the time was mocked. What I delivered was the fork
at GitHub - oxdev6/fiber: Fiber fork with SwapAdvertisement for RGB++ (feat/swap-advertisement) · GitHub on branch feat/swap-advertisement:
SwapAdvertisement as a real gossip message with signing and expiry, the
discovery index, the RPC and CLI, and the tests. That testing ran against CKB
testnet (chain hash
0x10639e0895502b5688a6be8cf69460d76541bfa4821629d86d62ba0aae3f9606 is in the
node_info output), and every rate, signature and expiry in the logs was
generated by the nodes at publish time. The notice’s own Related Links line
still points to Cell Sandbox with “placeholder — please confirm”, which is a
different project, so I suspect the review file was assembled from an old link.
Both of those are arguments about process. The finding I cannot argue with is
the substantive one: at close there was no swap, and nothing swap-level had
been run on a public network. That was the project’s stated purpose and it was
not there. So I built it.
On 20 October, on testnet3, with an asset issued for the run:
issuance: Bitcoin mempool - Bitcoin Explorer
and CKB https://testnet.explorer.nervos.org/transaction/0xfc29fb99fb07a237e4736a7dac0122ec43c78459d6f460d3858d5b5e796bf671
leap into the BTC time lock: Bitcoin mempool - Bitcoin Explorer
and CKB https://testnet.explorer.nervos.org/transaction/0x958d8fab158551f19b3f83d66c9c2fddc7e46f4d1a0867a4515420973c245f1b
unlock using the SPV proof of that Bitcoin transaction:
https://testnet.explorer.nervos.org/transaction/0xe9fb7df0aa465c3d6e605244ab3551b93dbad53c1b7550b92950d02d324f91ef
transfer into the trading node:
https://testnet.explorer.nervos.org/transaction/0xe5eb776a53b360aa14378d319726a05bca3a8683c004379185fa10cec9909ed1
a Fiber channel carrying that exact asset
(0xbdfbc4511046bbef056bd3173b9a10083b898f734b660cd16b4f39c13d9a4cf8), an
advertisement at rate 100, and a swap that settled: 1 unit of the asset for
100 CKB, order
0x2823d3ec5242502c2e0d3303663c56ff91ba765ad3144e462fc8de8d3b67cdb0, status
Success.
The full record is at
fiber-rgbpp-swap/docs/submission.md at main · oxdev6/fiber-rgbpp-swap · GitHub. To
check it without trusting the write-up, clone the repo and run
bash scripts/verify-evidence.sh: it queries the public CKB and Bitcoin
testnet APIs for all six transactions, prints the block heights, and exits
non-zero if anything is missing.
Two claims in the original proposal were overstated, and I would rather correct
them than defend them. The swap is atomic: one invoice, one payment hash, both
legs settle or the hub refunds. The leap is not atomic with it, because a cell
cannot carry the RGB++ lock and a channel lock at the same time, so the
conversion is a separate on-chain step that precedes the swap. “Conversion and
swap composed so that they succeed or fail together” is not achievable without
changing the lock model, and I should have said that in the proposal instead of
writing it as a goal. On the refund path, validation failures are covered live
(rate mismatch, expired advertisement, unknown advertisement, all rejected with
no funds moved) and the timeout handling is unit-tested; I did not stage a live
mid-flight timeout.
So the request: judge the project against the $1,000 baseline, and release the
outstanding amount.
Carl (@oxdev6)

topics.title: Twine: Buy and Sell CKB Without Depositing on an Exchange (Fiber P2P PoC)

recent_posts.topic_title: Twine: Buy and Sell CKB Without Depositing on an Exchange (Fiber P2P PoC)
recent_posts.author: ebubedev
recent_posts.content_text:
Update: sell-only book, and JIT inbound at release
1. The book is sell-only
A post offers CKB. The poster is the seller. The taker is the buyer. There is no buy post.
The last build had both sides: sell (offering CKB) and buy (bidding for CKB). A buy post made the taker the seller. take had no invoice. Both sides got need-invoice, and the buyer sent payout-invoice before any hold existed.
That path is gone.
new-order with side other than sell is refused.
Taking a leftover buy post is refused.
take always carries the buyer’s payout invoice. The hold is created there. No need-invoice round trip on take.
The app no longer has Buy / Sell tabs. Posts is one list of sell offers. A buy post on the relay is hidden.
New post has no side picker. It always sells. Confirm is Sell CKB?
You buy CKB by taking someone else’s sell. You sell by posting.
sequenceDiagram
autonumber
participant BN as Buyer node
participant B as Buyer
participant D as Daemon
participant O as Operator node
participant S as Seller
S->>D: new-order (sell)
BN->>BN: mint S_b, invoice under H(S_b)
B->>D: take with that invoice
D->>O: hold under H(S_b), no preimage
D-->>S: pay-invoice
D-->>B: pay-invoice
Note over O: no S_b, so no settle and no force-close claim
S->>O: pays the hold
O-->>D: Received
D-->>B: waiting-fiat
D-->>S: waiting-fiat
B->>S: fiat, outside Twine
B->>D: fiat-sent
S->>D: release
D->>D: record the hash before paying
D->>O: send_payment
O->>BN: pays H(S_b)
O-->>D: payment_preimage is S_b
D->>O: create_preimage, then settle
D-->>B: settled
D-->>S: settled
2. JIT inbound at release
A Fiber payment needs inbound on the receiver. Capacity is not inbound. A channel the buyer funds alone cannot receive. Asking every buyer to dual-fund a channel before they take a small trade is a bad first step, especially on a laptop with no public IP.
On release, if Twine cannot already pay the buyer, the daemon opens a private one-way channel to them, funded from the Twine Fiber node.
That is JIT inbound. It happens at payout, not at take.
sequenceDiagram
autonumber
participant S as Seller
participant D as Daemon
participant O as Twine Fiber
participant B as Buyer node
S->>D: release
D->>O: list_channels toward buyer
alt outbound already covers the trade
D->>O: send_payment
else no inbound
D->>O: connect_peer if needed
D->>O: open_channel one_way, private, trade + reserve, min 100 CKB
O-->>B: channel confirms
D->>O: send_payment
end
O-->>D: payment_preimage is S_b
D->>O: create_preimage, then settle
If the buyer already has inbound, Twine pays and does not open. If they are already peered, it does not dial again. If the node is offline, it does not hang on the hold. It asks for a new invoice. The buyer reconnects, stays online, and retries. A pending open is not paid twice.
The hub now publishes its listen addresses on kind 31421. Take can include a public Fiber listen address. Loopback and LAN addresses are refused. A laptop connects outbound to the hub. It does not need a public IP.
What you do
Role
Before the trade
At payout
Seller
Post the offer. Open and fund a channel to the Twine hub so you can lock the hold.
Release, same as before.
Buyer
Take that sell. Connect outbound to the hub. Leave auto-accept on. Keep about 99 CKB on-chain.
Stay online. Twine opens inbound to you if you cannot receive yet.
The app says this on Post, Take, and Trade. Post and Take show a channel checklist. Seller has to confirm outbound before they can post or take. Buyer is told to stay online so Twine can open inbound at payout.
What this spends
The Twine node now spends on-chain CKB to fund those channels. Keep spare CKB on it. The RPC biscuit grew: read / write on channels and peers, on top of invoices, payments, node, and watchtower.
read("node");
read("invoices"); write("invoices");
read("payments"); write("payments");
read("channels"); write("channels");
read("peers"); write("peers");
write("watchtower");
node("<this fnn pubkey>");
A one-way channel only lets the opener send. Twine is the opener. A buyer-funded one-way still cannot receive.
3. Deploy
There is a VPS install path: DEPLOY.md. Fiber 0.9.1, port 8228 public, RPC on localhost, systemd for the daemon. The README covers the CKB key, the biscuit, and announced_addrs for wallets that are not on the same machine.
What this does not change
Fiat is still off the protocol.
The daemon still stores no preimage at take.
A failed payout still does not settle. The buyer can still send another invoice with the same payment hash.
The 36-hour hold, the 15-minute payment window, and the 30-minute safety margin are the same.
Disputes are the same.
Tests (cargo test in the daemon, mock Fiber)
a_buy_post_cannot_be_created_or_taken
a_post_must_be_sell
payout_skips_jit_when_the_buyer_already_has_inbound
payout_opens_a_one_way_channel_when_the_buyer_has_no_inbound
payout_skips_connect_when_the_buyer_already_peered
payout_asks_for_a_new_invoice_when_the_buyer_node_is_offline
a_buyer_funded_one_way_channel_cannot_receive
operator_funded_one_way_can_pay
The app tests that Buy / Sell tabs are gone, that a buy post is hidden, and that the buyer checklist is JIT inbound at payout.
Code
Daemon: github.com/chukwuma619/twine
App: github.com/chukwuma619/twine_app
Ask for review
@ArthurZhang @quake — please look at this JIT path. The hold hash is still the buyer’s. The new piece is that the operator node now opens a private one-way channel at release when there is no route.
I want blunt notes on:
Opening at release, not at take. The buyer has to stay online through an on-chain channel open while the hold is already Received.
Funding with trade + 99 CKB reserve, floored at 100 CKB so a default Fiber node auto-accepts. one_way: true, public: false.
The biscuit now includes write("channels") and write("peers").
If the open is slow, the 30-minute safety margin can still refund the seller after fiat was marked sent.
Anything I am missing on Fiber auto-accept, one-way channels, or a laptop that only connected outbound.

recent_posts.author: Victor_Okenwa
recent_posts.content_text:
Ever wanted to customize your connect wallet and found it hard, or you just don’t know how? Now you have the answer you’ve been looking for. You already own the CCC provider. What you have been missing is a connect flow you can shape: which wallets appear, how a single row looks, and what the person sees after they connect. Icon, name, address, balance, or a did:ckb profile. Your layout. Your classes. image579×784 28 KB What you get A connect button that disappears once a wallet is connected, so your own layout can take its place A dialog you fill yourself: wallet list, chain choice, connecting state, then the account A wallet list you can narrow to the names you support, or leave open to every wallet CCC finds One row you can restyle without touching the others Icon only, name only, or both An account view you compose: wallet profile, or a did:ckb avatar, name, and identifier Disconnect and switch network, placed where you want them Balance digits that truncate instead of round, and an address you shorten from both ends Leave the dialog out and open() still opens CCC. Mount it, and that same click opens yours. Install npm install ckb-connect-wallet-kit @ckb-ccc/connector-react react react-dom Tailwind v4 does not scan node_modules until you point it at the package: @import "tailwindcss"; @source "../node_modules/ckb-connect-wallet-kit/dist"; Sit the kit under the ccc.Provider you already have. The kit never mounts CCC. The dialog is yours ConnectWalletDialog does not draw a popup by itself. You decide the chrome. ConnectWalletDialogOverlay is the centered modal. Skip it and the same steps can live in a drawer, a dropdown, or a page. open below comes from useConnectWallet(). The connect button calls it. Any element you write can call it too.

Connect Wallet

 connected-account1152×864 94.1 KB One signer connects immediately. Several signers move to the chain step. After a successful connect the dialog stays on the account step. Disconnect brings the wallet list back. After they connect This is the account step: the connected wallet dialog. Put the header, the profile, and the footer in the order your product needs. image563×412 12.7 KB With did:ckb Wrap the account body in ConnectWalletDid. The avatar, display name, and identifier come from the lock’s did:ckb profile. Each piece takes a fallback, so a wallet with no DID still has something to show. } /> } /> Nothing is fetched until you render ConnectWalletDid. Wallet profile Skip DID and show the wallet itself: icon, name, address, balance. The same pieces work outside the dialog. A button that calls open() can be the profile on your page, and the dialog can be the place they manage the account. Which wallets, and how they look Omit wallets and the list is every wallet CCC discovers. Pass names when you only want the wallets you support, in that order. A name that is not installed is skipped. show is "both", "icon", or "name". An icon-only row keeps the wallet name as its accessible label. Style every row the same way with buttonClassName. Style one wallet with ConnectWalletDialogWallet, or with the class the list already puts on each row. That class is the CCC name, lowercased, with other characters turned into -, prefixed by ckb-wallet-. MetaMask is ckb-wallet-metamask. JoyID Passkey is ckb-wallet-joyid-passkey. Or draw the rows yourself:
Links npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/ckb-connect-wallet-kit Demo: https://ckb-connect-wallet-kit.vercel.app/ Usage, with a live result for each of these layouts: ckb-connect-wallet-kit Repository: GitHub - Victor-Okenwa/revamp-ckb-connect-wallet: A compound component of the CKB connect wallet to improve developer experience. · GitHub If a snippet here does not click, open the usage page. Each row tells you whether you need to be connected or disconnected, then shows the result next to the code. If something is awkward, missing, or wrong, say so. A short note on the usage page, or an issue, is enough: Issues · Victor-Okenwa/revamp-ckb-connect-wallet · GitHub

You already own the CCC provider. What you have been missing is a connect flow you can shape: which wallets appear, how a single row looks, and what the person sees after they connect. Icon, name, address, balance, or a did:ckb profile. Your layout. Your classes.

image579×784 28 KB

What you get

  • A connect button that disappears once a wallet is connected, so your own layout can take its place

  • A dialog you fill yourself: wallet list, chain choice, connecting state, then the account

  • A wallet list you can narrow to the names you support, or leave open to every wallet CCC finds

  • One row you can restyle without touching the others

  • Icon only, name only, or both

  • An account view you compose: wallet profile, or a did:ckb avatar, name, and identifier

  • Disconnect and switch network, placed where you want them

  • Balance digits that truncate instead of round, and an address you shorten from both ends

Leave the dialog out and open() still opens CCC. Mount it, and that same click opens yours.

Install

npm install ckb-connect-wallet-kit @ckb-ccc/connector-react react react-dom

Tailwind v4 does not scan node_modules until you point it at the package:

@import "tailwindcss";
@source "../node_modules/ckb-connect-wallet-kit/dist";

Sit the kit under the ccc.Provider you already have. The kit never mounts CCC.

The dialog is yours

ConnectWalletDialog does not draw a popup by itself. You decide the chrome. ConnectWalletDialogOverlay is the centered modal. Skip it and the same steps can live in a drawer, a dropdown, or a page.

open below comes from useConnectWallet(). The connect button calls it. Any element you write can call it too.

<ConnectWalletContainer>
  <ConnectWalletButton />
  <ConnectWalletDialog>
    <ConnectWalletDialogOverlay>
      <ConnectWalletDialogWallets>
        <ConnectWalletDialogWalletsHeader>
          <h2>Connect Wallet</h2>
          <ConnectWalletDialogClose />
        </ConnectWalletDialogWalletsHeader>
        <ConnectWalletDialogWalletList />
        <ConnectWalletDialogWalletsFooter>
          <ConnectWalletDialogWalletsRefresh />
        </ConnectWalletDialogWalletsFooter>
      </ConnectWalletDialogWallets>
      <ConnectWalletDialogSigners />
      <ConnectWalletDialogConnecting />
      <ConnectWalletDialogAccount>
        <ConnectWalletDialogAccountHeader>
          <ConnectWalletName />
          <ConnectWalletDialogClose />
        </ConnectWalletDialogAccountHeader>
        <ConnectWalletAddress />
        <ConnectWalletBalance />
      </ConnectWalletDialogAccount>
    </ConnectWalletDialogOverlay>
  </ConnectWalletDialog>
</ConnectWalletContainer>

connected-account1152×864 94.1 KB

One signer connects immediately. Several signers move to the chain step. After a successful connect the dialog stays on the account step. Disconnect brings the wallet list back.

After they connect

This is the account step: the connected wallet dialog. Put the header, the profile, and the footer in the order your product needs.

image563×412 12.7 KB

With did:ckb

Wrap the account body in ConnectWalletDid. The avatar, display name, and identifier come from the lock’s did:ckb profile. Each piece takes a fallback, so a wallet with no DID still has something to show.

<ConnectWalletDialogAccount>
  <ConnectWalletDialogAccountHeader>
    <ConnectWalletName />
    <ConnectWalletDialogClose />
  </ConnectWalletDialogAccountHeader>
  <ConnectWalletDid>
    <ConnectWalletDidAvatar
      className="h-16 w-16"
      fallback={<ConnectWalletImage className="h-16 w-16 rounded-2xl" />}
    />
    <ConnectWalletDidName fallback={<ConnectWalletAddress frontChars={6} endChars={4} />} />
    <ConnectWalletDidId />
    <ConnectWalletBalance />
  </ConnectWalletDid>
  <ConnectWalletDialogAccountFooter>
    <ConnectWalletDisconnect />
    <ConnectWalletSwitchNetwork />
  </ConnectWalletDialogAccountFooter>
</ConnectWalletDialogAccount>

Nothing is fetched until you render ConnectWalletDid.

Wallet profile

Skip DID and show the wallet itself: icon, name, address, balance.

<ConnectWalletDialogAccount>
  <ConnectWalletDialogAccountHeader>
    <ConnectWalletImage />
    <ConnectWalletName />
    <ConnectWalletDialogClose />
  </ConnectWalletDialogAccountHeader>
  <ConnectWalletAddress frontChars={6} endChars={4} />
  <ConnectWalletBalance decimalPlaces={4} />
  <ConnectWalletDialogAccountFooter>
    <ConnectWalletDisconnect buttonText="Disconnect" />
    <ConnectWalletSwitchNetwork />
  </ConnectWalletDialogAccountFooter>
</ConnectWalletDialogAccount>

The same pieces work outside the dialog. A button that calls open() can be the profile on your page, and the dialog can be the place they manage the account.

Which wallets, and how they look

Omit wallets and the list is every wallet CCC discovers.

<ConnectWalletDialogWalletList />

Pass names when you only want the wallets you support, in that order. A name that is not installed is skipped.

<ConnectWalletDialogWalletList wallets={["JoyID", "MetaMask"]} />

show is "both", "icon", or "name". An icon-only row keeps the wallet name as its accessible label.

<ConnectWalletDialogWalletList show="icon" />

Style every row the same way with buttonClassName. Style one wallet with ConnectWalletDialogWallet, or with the class the list already puts on each row. That class is the CCC name, lowercased, with other characters turned into -, prefixed by ckb-wallet-. MetaMask is ckb-wallet-metamask. JoyID Passkey is ckb-wallet-joyid-passkey.

<ConnectWalletDialogWalletList className="[&_.ckb-wallet-joyid]:border-emerald-400 [&_.ckb-wallet-joyid]:bg-emerald-400/10" />

Or draw the rows yourself:

<div className="flex flex-col gap-2">
  <ConnectWalletDialogWallet name="JoyID" className="border-emerald-400 bg-emerald-400/10" />
  <ConnectWalletDialogWallet name="MetaMask" />
</div>

Links

  • npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/ckb-connect-wallet-kit

  • Demo: https://ckb-connect-wallet-kit.vercel.app/

  • Usage, with a live result for each of these layouts: ckb-connect-wallet-kit

  • Repository: GitHub - Victor-Okenwa/revamp-ckb-connect-wallet: A compound component of the CKB connect wallet to improve developer experience. · GitHub

If a snippet here does not click, open the usage page. Each row tells you whether you need to be connected or disconnected, then shows the result next to the code.

If something is awkward, missing, or wrong, say so. A short note on the usage page, or an issue, is enough: Issues · Victor-Okenwa/revamp-ckb-connect-wallet · GitHub

recent_posts.content_text:
GM @xingtianchunyan,
Thank you to you and the Spark Program Committee for reviewing the Corven proposal and providing an opportunity to clarify these concerns.
I would like to clarify that the decision to hold the first session remotely was made due to the lack of funds available to facilitate my travel to the event location in Kisumu. Rather than postpone or cancel the planned engagement, I decided to proceed remotely and coordinate the session alongside the Kisumu event organized by Umoja Verse. This allowed the community engagement activities to move forward despite the logistical limitations.
1. Scope of coverage for remote meetings and physical events
The original proposal was designed around physical community engagement sessions. The first session was conducted remotely as an adjustment to the available resources, not as a change to the overall implementation plan.
With the requested grant funding, I intend to hold the subsequent planned meetings physically, as initially proposed. The funding would help facilitate travel to the event locations and provide necessary mobile data support for participants where applicable. These resources are important for enabling direct engagement, hands-on demonstrations, collaborative experimentation, and practical support for developers using Corven IDE.
I will revise the budget to distinguish between the costs associated with the first remote session and those required to facilitate the remaining physical meetings. Any expenses that are no longer applicable to the first session will be adjusted accordingly, while the necessary and justified costs for the planned physical activities will remain in the budget.
2. Feasibility of the proposed goals
I believe the original targets remain achievable, particularly if the remaining sessions are conducted physically as planned. In-person meetings will provide better opportunities for guided experimentation, troubleshooting, collaboration, and direct feedback from participants.
The proposed targets remain:
More than 40 participants in total across the three meetings.
At least 70% of participants completing Experiment A.
At least 50% of participants completing Experiment B.
At least 80% of participants completing the post-meeting survey.
I will track attendance, experiment completion, and survey submissions to document progress against these targets. I will also use the feedback collected to assess Corven IDE’s usability and identify areas for improvement.
The remote first session demonstrates my commitment to maintaining progress even when logistical challenges arise. However, the remaining physical sessions would benefit from the requested funding, which would enable implementation closer to the original proposal.
I will update the proposal and budget to reflect this clarification and ensure that the implementation plan, costs, and targets are aligned.

recent_posts.author: xingtianchunyan
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi @Chaichamp,
Thank you for taking the time to revise the proposal based on our previous feedback, and for your continued efforts to refine the MatchLock concept.
The committee has completed its review. After careful discussion, we regret to inform you that we have decided not to approve the MatchLock project at this time.
We’d like to be candid about the reasons behind this decision:
Existing ecosystem infrastructure already adequately supports this primitive: Commit-reveal is a fundamental cryptographic primitive already used by nearly every project on CKB—and across the broader blockchain ecosystem. The core code for a hash commitment scheme is only a few lines, and existing libraries already handle it well. In the committee’s view, packaging it as a third-party library that other projects would have to adopt would add an extra dependency without delivering clear additional value over existing foundational components.
We greatly appreciate all the effort your team has put in. The committee hopes that you and your team will give greater consideration to the specific needs that exist in the community and propose solutions that genuinely address them. Keep building, and feel free to reach out anytime!
Best regards,
Xingtian
On behalf of the Spark Program Committee
CC: @Hanssen @yixiu.ckbfans.bit @zz_tovarishch

By FidelCoder |

Venue preview (posted one day before): Umojaverse on X: "Kisumu, take a look at tomorrow’s playground Today, it’s a venue. Tomorrow, it’s YOU, laptops open, questions flying, and builders meeting builders. @NervosNetwork @Zone01Kisumu who’s pulling up? Get in the room https://t.co/khDmxipeRR" / X

X: Umojaverse on X: "Exciting day... we're started for the day. We're eating CKB for breakfast cc: @NervosNetwork" / X
TikTok: TikTok - Make Your Day
LinkedIn: #ckb #umojaverse | Umojaverse | Kisumu, let’s make CKB real. Meet @NervosNetwork at @Zone01Kisumu for… | Umojaverse
Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/p/DerpAAwCfKs/?rpxt=bWo2bTN4ZXF6ZTYy | https://www.instagram.com/reel/DeqkKeFgJDe/?exln=ODVzaGE5eWZhMW5q
Photo album (Google Drive): Highlights – Google Drive
Kisumu’s first CKB Builders Workshop brought 37 people into the room from 70 RSVPs. Eleven arrived with laptops ready for hands-on building, around 17 brought notebooks and pens to work through the sessions, and every attendee had a smartphone. That turnout is a meaningful starting point for a local builder community, and a reason to invest in what comes next.
The event at a glance
11920×1148 633 KB
RSVPs: 70
Attendees: 37
RSVP-to-attendance rate: 52.9%
Builders ready for hands-on work with laptops: About 11 (30% of attendees)
Builders following sessions with notebook and pen: About 17 (46% of attendees)
Attendees with smartphones: 37 (100%)
Why this workshop mattered
_DSC43401920×1280 640 KB
This was the first CKB workshop in the Kisumu region. It created a first local point of contact for developers and community builders to encounter CKB and Fiber through practical examples. The workshop built from familiar programming knowledge into CKB’s Cell model, a working transaction and Fiber’s invoice flow, making the ecosystem concrete for people who had not built on CKB before.
The 37-person turnout, including builders who arrived ready to work with laptops and participants who followed the sessions with notebook and pen, shows there is a strong base for continued technical learning in Kisumu. Every attendee had a smartphone, giving the group a shared way to stay connected to digital tools and follow-up activities. For an ecosystem working to grow beyond established developer hubs, that level of participation matters: it brings new builders into the conversation and creates a foundation for discovering and supporting products being built locally.
The workshop also connected technical learning to product judgement. Participants examined not only how a payment is submitted, but what evidence a merchant should check before marking an order paid. That connection between infrastructure, developer skills and real customer experience is important for builders who want to create useful applications on-chain and off-chain.
What we covered
_DSC42841920×1280 382 KB
We designed the sessions for developers who can learn technical material but may be encountering CKB for the first time. The workshop moved from fundamentals into practical code and product decisions:
CKB and the Cell model: how Cells hold capacity, how lock scripts control spending, and how transactions consume existing Cells and create new ones.
A CKB transfer: using CCC with a prepared OffCKB local development network to construct, sign, submit and inspect a transaction, including its inputs, merchant output, change and fee.
Fiber payments: how funds are committed to a payment channel on CKB, how channel balances update off-chain, and how a merchant invoice is created, paid and checked.
Checkout design: what the customer and merchant should see when an invoice is created, a payment is pending, a payment fails or the merchant confirms payment.
Builder next steps: reproducing the examples, improving documentation or reporting a reproducible bug, and continuing the merchant-checkout idea on testnet.
Panel discussion: when should checkout show “Paid”?
p1920×1280 628 KB
The panel discussion drew active participation, with attendees asking questions and engaging with the speakers. The conversation centred on the payment flow demonstrated during the workshop: what confirmation a merchant needs, how a checkout should represent a pending or unsuccessful payment, and what evidence should be checked before an order is marked paid. Audience questions brought practical developer and merchant perspectives into the discussion.
What’s next: CKB Productathon
The workshop created a foundation for continued product building in Kisumu and across Kenya.
Kisumu and other parts of Kenya already have ambitious builders working on products on-chain and off-chain. The next step is the CKB Productathon, a programme for early-stage products, products ready to scale and promising new projects with the potential to become startups.
The Productathon is intended to carry teams beyond a coding sprint or an MVP. It would help them validate real user needs, improve and test their products, and plan for pilots, growth and long-term sustainability. I’m seeking CKB ecosystem support to shape and deliver this next step, including technical mentorship and practical support that helps teams continue after the programme. I welcome a conversation with CKB about developing the format, timeline and outcomes together.
Acknowledgements
I’m grateful to the Zone01 Kisumu team for their support and partnership, and to the speakers, facilitators, learners and community builders who made the workshop possible.

Kisumu’s first CKB Builders Workshop brought 37 people into the room from 70 RSVPs. Eleven arrived with laptops ready for hands-on building, around 17 brought notebooks and pens to work through the sessions, and every attendee had a smartphone. That turnout is a meaningful starting point for a local builder community, and a reason to invest in what comes next.

The event at a glance

11920×1148 633 KB

  • RSVPs: 70

  • Attendees: 37

  • RSVP-to-attendance rate: 52.9%

  • Builders ready for hands-on work with laptops: About 11 (30% of attendees)

  • Builders following sessions with notebook and pen: About 17 (46% of attendees)

  • Attendees with smartphones: 37 (100%)

Why this workshop mattered

_DSC43401920×1280 640 KB

This was the first CKB workshop in the Kisumu region. It created a first local point of contact for developers and community builders to encounter CKB and Fiber through practical examples. The workshop built from familiar programming knowledge into CKB’s Cell model, a working transaction and Fiber’s invoice flow, making the ecosystem concrete for people who had not built on CKB before.

The 37-person turnout, including builders who arrived ready to work with laptops and participants who followed the sessions with notebook and pen, shows there is a strong base for continued technical learning in Kisumu. Every attendee had a smartphone, giving the group a shared way to stay connected to digital tools and follow-up activities. For an ecosystem working to grow beyond established developer hubs, that level of participation matters: it brings new builders into the conversation and creates a foundation for discovering and supporting products being built locally.

The workshop also connected technical learning to product judgement. Participants examined not only how a payment is submitted, but what evidence a merchant should check before marking an order paid. That connection between infrastructure, developer skills and real customer experience is important for builders who want to create useful applications on-chain and off-chain.

What we covered

_DSC42841920×1280 382 KB

We designed the sessions for developers who can learn technical material but may be encountering CKB for the first time. The workshop moved from fundamentals into practical code and product decisions:

  • CKB and the Cell model: how Cells hold capacity, how lock scripts control spending, and how transactions consume existing Cells and create new ones.

  • A CKB transfer: using CCC with a prepared OffCKB local development network to construct, sign, submit and inspect a transaction, including its inputs, merchant output, change and fee.

  • Fiber payments: how funds are committed to a payment channel on CKB, how channel balances update off-chain, and how a merchant invoice is created, paid and checked.

  • Checkout design: what the customer and merchant should see when an invoice is created, a payment is pending, a payment fails or the merchant confirms payment.

  • Builder next steps: reproducing the examples, improving documentation or reporting a reproducible bug, and continuing the merchant-checkout idea on testnet.

Panel discussion: when should checkout show “Paid”?

p1920×1280 628 KB

The panel discussion drew active participation, with attendees asking questions and engaging with the speakers. The conversation centred on the payment flow demonstrated during the workshop: what confirmation a merchant needs, how a checkout should represent a pending or unsuccessful payment, and what evidence should be checked before an order is marked paid. Audience questions brought practical developer and merchant perspectives into the discussion.

What’s next: CKB Productathon

The workshop created a foundation for continued product building in Kisumu and across Kenya.

Kisumu and other parts of Kenya already have ambitious builders working on products on-chain and off-chain. The next step is the CKB Productathon, a programme for early-stage products, products ready to scale and promising new projects with the potential to become startups.

The Productathon is intended to carry teams beyond a coding sprint or an MVP. It would help them validate real user needs, improve and test their products, and plan for pilots, growth and long-term sustainability. I’m seeking CKB ecosystem support to shape and deliver this next step, including technical mentorship and practical support that helps teams continue after the programme. I welcome a conversation with CKB about developing the format, timeline and outcomes together.

Acknowledgements

I’m grateful to the Zone01 Kisumu team for their support and partnership, and to the speakers, facilitators, learners and community builders who made the workshop possible.

Hi @AI_Ttimes,
Thank you for taking the time to prepare and submit the Fiber Mystery Shopper proposal. The committee has completed its review, and after careful consideration, it has regrettably decided not to approve Fiber Mystery Shopper at this stage.
We would like to explain frankly the reasons behind this decision:
The actual needs have not been clearly established: Although the August report did mention that “individual users, duplicate payments, and recovery tests can provide useful evidence,” the committee believes that the proposal merely focuses on “collecting more data,” without specifying which specific and recurring problem this tool will help solve within the Fiber ecosystem. The current project appears to be a general testing effort rather than a response to a specific, unmet need.
The “evidence” generated has limited value in practical applications: The signature logs and pre-payment records produced by testing transactions can indeed be verified, but these tests are carried out only on the test network—where liquidity is scarce, there are no real economic incentives, and the behavior of node operators differs—as a result, it is not possible to provide evidence that the committee can rely on when applying it to the main network environment.
I am extremely grateful for all the efforts put in by your team. I hope you will think more deeply to identify the true needs. I also encourage you to continue working on this, and feel free to contact me at any time!
Yours sincerely,
xingtian
On behalf of the Spark Program Committee

Hi @Ticoworld,
Thank you for taking the time to submit the proposal, and for sharing the detailed project overview, GitHub repository, and clear technical reasoning behind RGB++ Resume.
The committee has completed its review and, after careful discussion, regrets to reject the RGB++ Resume project at this time.
We want to be transparent about the reasoning behind this decision:
The demand is real, but third-party involvement in transfer stability is risky: The committee acknowledges that interrupted RGB++ transfers are a genuine pain point, and we appreciate your thoughtful analysis of the problem space—particularly the flowchart demonstrating how an app can lose state across wallet handoffs and restarts. However, recovery of interrupted RGB++ transfers touches the stability and correctness of the transfer flow itself. The committee believes this is a core responsibility that should not be delegated to a third-party service or library, as failures in this layer could directly impact user funds and undermine confidence in the RGB++ ecosystem.
Thank you very much for all the hard work your team has put in. Keep building, and feel free to reach out anytime!

2026 October 20, Fourth Weekly Report
Introduction to Qubes-OS and how to handle the forwarding of network traffic between SystemApp-Qubes:
We need IP of:
destination Qube
sys-firewall
sys-net
forward/NAT Port in sys-net and sys-firewall
allow Port in destination Qube
allow Router TCP Port to LAN-IP of sys-net
Note: To have the rules persistant, even after system-restart, it must be configured in the Disposable-Template of NetQubes. I haven’t made it persistent yet, which is why it’s not included in today’s description here.
In dom0 (Xfce Terminal in dom0) execute:
qvm-ls -n
Now the row “IP” shows the Qube-Network address. You can compare with Terminal of destination-Qube (look at eth0):
ip -4 -br a | grep UP
The physical sys-net IP looks like: 192.168.178.88:8115/TCP - (internal sys-net IP: 10.137.0.8).
Now we need IP of sys-firewall and destination-App-Qube. Execute in dom0:
qvm-ls -n
Name of the physical Interface in sys-net
sys-firewall-ip: 10.138.4.89 - IP destination-Qube: 10.137.0.9
Also check that the destination-Qube really uses sys-firewall as NetVM. In dom0 execute:
qvm-prefs DESTINATION-QUBE netvm
If there is written “sys-firewall” we continue.
For the name of the phsysical Network-Interface, open Terminal in sys-net and execute:
ip -4 -br a
The name is the one that is written at the very left at row 192.168.178.88 e.g. eth0, NOT the one thats beginning with vif.
DNAT-CHAIN in Qubes 4.3.2:
We use a chain in “sys-net” in the table “ip cubes”, a rule with fitting entry-Interface and a optional source-IP in combination with a fitting forward-rule. In “sys-firewall” forward a connection over “iifgroup 1”.
After executing the commands we can see the acutal condition by executing
sudo nft list table ip qubes
Open Terminal in “sys-net” to find the Name of the physical Interface and execute:
ip -4 -br a | grep UP
Open another Terminal in “sys-net” and execute this three commands (here without restriction to a specific source-IP) - Also here: This Rules are not persistent after a restart. To make them persistent, we’d need to add them to sys-net and sys-firewall in “/rw/config/qubes-firewall-user-script”.
sudo nft add chain qubes custom-dnat-port8115 '{ type nat hook prerouting priority filter +1 ; policy accept; }'
sudo nft add rule qubes custom-dnat-port8115 iifname "INTERFACE_NAME" tcp dport 8115 ct state new,established,related counter dnat SYS_FIREWALL_IP
sudo nft add rule qubes custom-forward iifname "INTERFACE_NAME" ip daddr SYS_FIREWALL_IP tcp dport 8115 ct state new,established,related counter accept
Open Terminal “sys-firewall” and also execute this three commands:
sudo nft add chain qubes custom-dnat-port8115 '{ type nat hook prerouting priority filter +1 ; policy accept; }'
sudo nft add rule qubes custom-dnat-port8115 iifgroup 1 tcp dport 8115 ct state new,established,related counter dnat DESTINATION_IP
sudo nft add rule qubes custom-forward iifgroup 1 ip daddr DESTINATION_IP tcp dport 8115 ct state new,established,related counter accept
Note: sys-firewall uses iifgroup 1 for recceiving traffic from sys-net. You can check in every NetQube if the rule-counters are rising:
nft list table ip qubes
Now Add in destination-Qube (10.137.0.9) an incoming Rule for TCP-Port 8115 (again, till now only valid till System-restart):
sudo nft add rule qubes custom-input tcp dport 8115 ip daddr 10.137.0.7 ct state new,established,related counter accept
With sudo nft list table ip qubes you can than see it there as “chain custom-input”.
On the graphical user interface (Xfce desktop), you’ll find “Qube Tools” in the menu, and then “[dom0] Qube Manager” there. Select your Destination_Qube e.g. “work” and than open “Settings”. There you can change the “Private storage max size:” to a high number, e.g. 690 GiB. Then click “Apply” to confirm. This Qube needs space because our blockchain is stored here.
Next, we have to add a rule to our network router to forward the port. Port 8115 must be allowed to connect to the IP address of our network node. Look under “Filter Rules” or in your router’s user manual for “Port Forwarding.”
We can now open the destination-Qube to download CKB, than init CKB maninet chain, customize ckb.toml and finally run CKB.

Now Add in destination-Qube (10.137.0.9) an incoming Rule for TCP-Port 8115 (again, till now only valid till System-restart):

  • sudo nft add rule qubes custom-input tcp dport 8115 ip daddr 10.137.0.7 ct state new,established,related counter accept

With sudo nft list table ip qubes you can than see it there as “chain custom-input”.

On the graphical user interface (Xfce desktop), you’ll find “Qube Tools” in the menu, and then “[dom0] Qube Manager” there. Select your Destination_Qube e.g. “work” and than open “Settings”. There you can change the “Private storage max size:” to a high number, e.g. 690 GiB. Then click “Apply” to confirm. This Qube needs space because our blockchain is stored here.

Next, we have to add a rule to our network router to forward the port. Port 8115 must be allowed to connect to the IP address of our network node. Look under “Filter Rules” or in your router’s user manual for “Port Forwarding.”

We can now open the destination-Qube to download CKB, than init CKB maninet chain, customize ckb.toml and finally run CKB.

topics.title: From CKB transactions to wallet connections: three design lessons from CCC

recent_posts.topic_title: From CKB transactions to wallet connections: three design lessons from CCC
recent_posts.author: zz_tovarishch
recent_posts.content_text:
Sending 100 CKB sounds simple: choose a recipient, enter the amount, and sign. For a DApp developer, that means deciding which cells to spend, creating the recipient’s output and any change, calculating a fee, and getting the transaction signed through the user’s wallet. Those pieces depend on one another. Adding inputs changes the transaction’s size, and the size changes the fee. Different wallets can also require different signing steps.
CKBers’ Codebase (CCC) is a TypeScript SDK that helps applications handle these details. Our work, When EVM Defaults Break: Three SDK Patterns for UTXO-Family Wallets, draws three design lessons from the work already done in CCC. It is a collaboration between CKBA’s DevRel and Ecosystem support teams, co-authored by @Hanssen (CCC core developer and first author) and @zz_tovarishch.
The starting point: a CKB transaction needs more than a recipient and an amount. In the familiar EVM flow using an externally owned account, an application can construct a transaction without selecting individual spendable outputs. CKB uses cells: UTXO-like units that hold state and are guarded by scripts. Each output cell also needs enough capacity to cover the space it occupies. The application therefore has to account for both the value being transferred and the capacity required by the resulting cells.
nervos_talk_fig_approach1813×1158 115 KB
The diagram summarizes the paper’s comparison with a conventional EVM account-based flow. A, B, and C are three modules within CCC, not three steps that execute in order.
1. Describe the outputs, then let CCC complete the transaction.
The Transaction Composer starts with what the application wants to create. CCC’s completion helpers handle input capacity, change, and fees, so the application does not have to write its own capacity-balancing loop for this transfer.
Here is the paper’s 100 CKB example. It assumes ccc is imported, receiver is the recipient’s lock script, and signer is already available:
image1664×494 72.1 KB
The first two awaited calls complete the inputs and fee handling. The third signs and sends. The application describes the intended output, while CCC handles the dependent construction work. To try it yourself, the CCC Playground runs CCC code in the browser, and the CCC docs cover setup and the full API.
This shifts work into the SDK: the paper traces how CCC’s fee handling grew into seven related methods between July 2024 and August 2025, including different ways to route change.
These helpers are optional. Developers who need control over a particular transaction can still assemble its fields themselves. That balance is the paper’s central lesson: automate routine work while keeping the manual path available.
2. Give the application one signing interface across different kinds of wallets.
On CKB, a cell’s lock script defines how spending is authorized. Wallet integration can therefore involve more than different brands using the same signature scheme. The paper covers eight CCC wallet adapters spanning three signing primitives: secp256k1 ECDSA, WebAuthn passkeys, and Schnorr signatures through Nostr.
CCC puts their differences in message construction, witness encoding, and key management behind a shared Signer interface. Witnesses carry the data used to satisfy the transaction’s scripts, including signatures. An application can use the shared interface while each adapter handles its own signing conventions. The JoyID adapter, for example, handles CKB, Bitcoin, EVM, and Nostr signing paths.
There is a tradeoff: a common interface exposes a shared baseline of capabilities. Features specific to a signing scheme still need optional extensions. This is the paper’s most distinctive pattern. It is also relevant as account abstraction (ERC-4337) brings more signing options to EVM applications.
3. Reuse the wallet connection interface.
Before signing, a DApp has to find the wallet, request permission, handle account changes, and show a connection dialog. Repeating this work in each application also means maintaining it as wallet APIs change.
CCC provides a Web Component, @ckb-ccc/connector, and a React wrapper, @ckb-ccc/connector-react. The DApp declares which wallets to enable and uses the shared connection interface. This moves the recurring work of supporting those wallet APIs into the SDK. It also gives CCC’s maintainers an ongoing responsibility to keep the integrations working.
The paper identifies these patterns by looking back at CCC’s public releases and exported APIs from July 2024 to June 2026, tracing designs that recur across wallets or transaction types. At the June 10, 2026 cutoff, CCC had 18 published @ckb-ccc/* packages on npm, including the eight wallet adapters, and 13 human contributors. This is a retrospective case study. It does not measure whether developers integrate wallets faster or introduce fewer defects.
The wider question is how SDKs can support applications when transactions need explicit input and resource balancing, and wallets use different signing primitives. Other extended-UTXO ecosystems, such as Cardano, already have examples of declarative transaction composition and reusable connectors. Documenting CCC’s design makes CKB’s application-development experience available for that broader discussion.
The paper has been accepted as a poster at IEEE ICDLT 2026, the IEEE International Conference on Distributed Ledger Technologies, in Alcobaça, Portugal, on December 3-4. The conference brings together academia and industry, with organizers from Nova School of Business and Economics, NOVA Information Management School, and the IEEE Portugal Section. It is part of Blockchain.PT, a project funded through Portugal’s Recovery and Resilience Plan and the EU’s NextGenerationEU program. Hanssen plans to present it in person.
Thank you to Hanssen and everyone who has contributed to CCC. These design lessons come from the SDK that contributors have built and maintained, and we hope the paper gives more developers a way to understand and build on that work.
If you have used CCC, where do its helpers save you work, and where do you still need to take manual control? Feedback from wallet and DApp developers would help us understand which parts of the design need more attention. Please read the paper, explore the code, and cite the work if it is useful to your research. If you are attending ICDLT, come discuss it with Hanssen at the poster.
